identity.title: Glucocorticoid exposure / abrupt withdrawal, known adrenal disease, hyperpigmentation

technique.how: Ask about any glucocorticoid in the past year (oral, inhaled, intra-articular, high-potency topical, megestrol), dose/duration, recent taper or missed doses, known Addison's, hypopituitarism or adrenal metastases, and adrenal-suppressing drugs (ketoconazole, etomidate, checkpoint inhibitors, opioids). Inspect palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars and sun-exposed skin for hyperpigmentation.
technique.prerequisites: Medication reconciliation including OTC, injections and recent hospital courses.

interpretation.positive_finding: Recent steroid exposure/withdrawal or known adrenal disease in a hypotensive, hyponatremic or hypoglycemic patient makes adrenal crisis a must-treat diagnosis. Hyperpigmentation points to primary (ACTH-high) disease and was present in 76% of registry Addison's patients.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absent hyperpigmentation does not exclude secondary/tertiary insufficiency (steroid withdrawal, pituitary disease), where pigmentation does not occur. Absent steroid history does not exclude primary disease.
interpretation.pitfalls: Inhaled, topical, intra-articular steroids and megestrol are frequently missed; pigmentation is subtle in dark skin or blamed on sun. Hyperkalemia occurs only in primary adrenal insufficiency.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive → draw cortisol/ACTH and give stress-dose hydrocortisone before results; negative → do not withhold empiric steroids in vasopressor-refractory shock.

estimates.target_condition: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, established diagnosis) — hyperpigmentation ever observed (sensitivity only; no non-Addison comparison group)
estimates.population: 148 patients with Addison's disease in a South African national registry (questionnaire, folder and laboratory review), median age at diagnosis 34 y
estimates.reference_standard: Established clinical/biochemical diagnosis of Addison's disease from records
estimates.quote: Hyperpigmentation was observed in 76%, nausea and vomiting occurred in more than 40%, and weight loss was noted in 25%.

sources.citation: Bornstein SR, Allolio B, Arlt W, Barthel A, Don-Wauchope A, Hammer GD et al. Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism 2016.
Ross IL, Levitt NS. Addison's disease symptoms--a cross sectional study in urban South Africa. PloS one 2013.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not wait for history confirmation or cosyntropin testing before treating suspected adrenal crisis in shock.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Hypotension with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypoglycemia and any steroid exposure or adrenal disease: give hydrocortisone immediately and resuscitate (Endocrine Society guideline).
safety_scope.interobserver_note: History elements; no reliability data found.

extraction_notes: Guideline anchor PMID 26760044 confirmed (Endocrine Society 2016 primary adrenal insufficiency guideline; abstract is methodological, no diagnostic-accuracy numbers). Searches ('adrenal insufficiency hyperpigmentation sensitivity diagnosis'; 'Addison disease clinical presentation hyperpigmentation frequency patients') found no controlled diagnostic-accuracy study of steroid-exposure history or hyperpigmentation; no JAMA RCE exists for adrenal insufficiency. Ross & Levitt 2013 (PMID 23308244, PLoS One) is a registry case series giving the frequency of hyperpigmentation among established Addison's patients (0.76), entered as sensitivity-only with no specificity (no controls), hence partially_quantified. Important scope note: hyperpigmentation applies only to primary AI; glucocorticoid withdrawal causes secondary/tertiary AI without pigmentation, so the id bundles two mechanisms with different signs. Same abstract: loss of consciousness as a presenting feature 20% (95% CI 14–28%), shock 5% (CI 1.5–8.5%) (Abstract, Results).
